title: Abraham bargains (Genesis 18:16–33)
hookLine: fifty righteous? forty-five? ten? He argues with God for a city

lines: NAME A PRICE, COME DOWN A LITTLE.
cards: Haggle in a market, and you know the rhythm. You name a price. They name a price.
You come down a little; they come up a little. Somebody pretends to walk away. Now try it with God.
After the meal at Mamre, the visitors look out toward Sodom, down on the plain where Lot lives.

And God, the story says, decides not to hide from Abraham what is about to happen: the outcry against Sodom is great, and God is going down to see. The two others walk on. Abraham stays, and steps closer.

teach.b: His first words are a question: will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty righteous people in the city.
Then the line that sits at the center of the whole chapter, in the King James Bible: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Abraham is holding God to God's own justice.
And God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Then the haggling begins. Abraham knows exactly how bold he's being.
He says: "Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes." Dust: remember the garden. A creature of dust, arguing with his maker.
Each time God agrees, without a single complaint. Then the last one: oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once. Ten?
"I will not destroy it for ten's sake." And there Abraham stops. Notice two things.
He isn't only bargaining for Lot; Lot's name never comes up.
He's arguing for a whole city of strangers, wicked ones at that. And God never rebukes him for it. Abraham isn't the last to argue with God in the Bible.
Moses will plead for his people. Job will demand an answer. Whole psalms ask how long, O LORD.

teach.h: SHALL NOT THE JUDGE OF ALL THE EARTH DO RIGHT?
teach.b: The Bible keeps room for this kind of honest, bold prayer, right alongside thy will be done. The text says God stayed in the conversation until Abraham was done.

how: Many Christians pray intercessions for cities and nations in trouble, and many churches include prayers for the world and for places in the news in their weekly worship.

o: begging God to save only his nephew Lot
trading his flocks for land near Sodom
pleading with God, down from fifty to ten

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the Judge of all the earth

s: Abraham bargains only to save his nephew Lot
Lot's name never comes up. he argues for a whole city of strangers.
God agrees every time, without a single complaint.
"I will not destroy it for ten's sake."

games.q: you're Abraham. God has agreed to spare the city for fifty righteous people. what do you do?
o: keep asking: forty-five? forty? thirty? twenty? ten?
ask God to destroy it anyway.
games.why: he keeps going, all the way down to ten, knowing he is "but dust and ashes," and God agrees each time.

practice: Think of a place that's hurting, a city in the news, a neighborhood near you, a hospital ward, and hold the whole place in mind, strangers included.
If you pray, you can speak up for it as Abraham did, plainly, even stubbornly, and ask again. If you don't, hold it with the same stubborn care, and notice what you'd ask for if you could.

wordCard.voice: Abraham bargains. Fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten: a man of dust and ashes argues with God for a whole city, and God listens.

orig.note: Hebrew: righteous. Abraham asks whether the righteous will be swept away with the wicked.

carryVoice: Your line: you can argue with god. Even dust and ashes gets a hearing. Until tomorrow.
